title: World Young Scientist Summit 2026: Where science connects people across borders
section: A gathering of young scientists from around the world
text:
A gathering of young scientists from around the world
I was honoured to be selected to participate in the World Young Scientist Summit (WYSS) 2026, held in Wenzhou, Zhejiang Province, China. I am especially grateful to the Organization for Women in Science for the Developing World (OWSD) for nominating me for this opportunity.
Hosted by the China Association for Science and Technology (CAST), the Zhejiang Provincial People’s Government, and the World Association of Young Scientists (WAYS), the summit brought together nearly 800 scientists, educators, and entrepreneurs from more than 60 countries and regions. Under the theme “Gathering Talents Worldwide to Create a Better Future,” the summit focused on “Global Youth Action in the AI Era: Building a Sustainable Future.” It provided a platform to exchange ideas, explore the role of artificial intelligence in different fields, and discuss how international scientific collaboration can help address global challenges.

title: World Young Scientist Summit 2026: Where science connects people across borders
section: Day 1: Connecting young scientists and exploring global challenges
text:
Day 1: Connecting young scientists and exploring global challenges
The summit activities began on 23 October with the International Young Scientists’ Roundtable. The programme included an introduction to WAYS and WYSS, a young scientists’ sharing session, and interactive discussions on global challenges and the potential of artificial intelligence to address them.
What I particularly enjoyed was the opportunity to hear different perspectives from young scientists working in diverse fields and countries. Although our research interests and backgrounds differed, we shared a common interest in using science and technology to make a positive contribution to society. The discussions highlighted both the opportunities AI creates and the challenges we need to consider as it becomes part of more areas of our lives.

Rethinking scientific research in the age of AI
One of the most thought-provoking parts of the International Young Scientists’ Roundtable was the discussion on how scientific research is changing in the age of artificial intelligence. Several important points were raised about the responsibilities of young scientists, the role of AI in research, and the values that must remain at the heart of scientific progress.
One point that particularly stood out to me was the growing tendency to focus on producing polished manuscripts rather than on the quality of the scientific work itself. A well-written paper is important, but it should never become more important than sound scientific results, reliable data, and the proper validation of findings. These are the foundations of meaningful scientific progress. AI tools will continue to evolve, but the fundamental purpose of science remains unchanged: to explain and understand how the natural world works while building reliable, evidence-based knowledge.
The discussion also highlighted the importance of curiosity-driven research, scientific integrity, and collaboration across disciplines and national borders. Scientific progress depends not simply on producing more publications, but on asking meaningful questions, carefully validating results, and building knowledge that others can trust and build upon. In an increasingly connected world, collaboration across disciplines and countries is essential for addressing complex scientific challenges.
Another important point was the potential of AI to make science more accessible and inclusive. Language barriers and limited access to scientific resources can prevent researchers, particularly those in developing countries, from fully participating in global scientific activities. AI tools can help researchers improve their academic writing, translate scientific information into their own languages, and access scientific knowledge more quickly. These opportunities are particularly important for developing countries, enabling their researchers to engage more actively in global scientific programmes, contribute their own knowledge, and participate in scientific progress. By making knowledge more accessible and supporting communication across languages, AI has the potential to accelerate scientific progress worldwide.
However, the discussion also emphasised that AI should support scientific judgement, not replace the judgement of experts. Its use must be guided by research integrity and ethical responsibility. AI can be misused, for example, by generating fabricated references or misrepresenting scientific results. Such practices undermine the credibility of research and the trust placed in scientific publications. Researchers therefore have a responsibility to verify information, validate results, check references, and ensure that their work accurately represents the evidence.
For me, one of the key messages from this discussion was that technological progress alone does not guarantee scientific progress. AI can make research faster and scientific communication easier, but the reliability of scientific records, research ethics, and the integrity of researchers remain essential. As young scientists embrace the opportunities offered by AI, we must ensure that these tools strengthen scientific research rather than compromise the principles on which it is built.


An evening of Chinese hospitality
The first day concluded with the WYSS Welcome Dinner at Awailou Resort Hotel. It was a wonderful introduction to Chinese food, culture, and hospitality. The dinner featured a variety of traditional Chinese dishes, and our hosts took the time to introduce us to Wenzhou, its strengths, facilities, and areas of development.
At our table, we had the pleasure of meeting Zhang Benfeng, Vice Mayor of the Wenzhou Municipal People’s Government, and a former second-class inspector of the Zhejiang Provincial Association for Science and Technology. Their presence and the warm welcome extended by the hosts made the evening particularly memorable.
One thing that impressed me throughout the day was how carefully the organisers had considered communication. English translation headphones were provided during the sessions, while a dedicated interpreter assisted our table during the dinner, translating the hosts’ introductions and conversations.
Watching people from different countries connect, share ideas, and enjoy conversations despite speaking different languages was a special experience. It reminded me that language does not have to be a barrier when people are willing to connect and understand one another.
The first day set a wonderful tone for the summit. It was not only about science and technology; it was also about people, cultures, shared challenges, and the possibilities that emerge when we come together.

title: Beyond the Floodgates: Rethinking Alert Thresholds for Effective Flood Warning Systems
text:
The Kelani River with elevated water level (Photo Credit Priyanga Dilini Talagala, 5 June 2024)


In recent days, Sri Lanka has experienced severe floods, worsened by the arrival of the southwestern monsoon season. This seasonal weather pattern, which occurs between May and September, brings heavy rainfall to the southwest regions of the country. Consequently, adverse weather conditions have caused widespread damage across multiple areas, disrupting lives and resulting in significant losses. While natural disasters can be unpredictable, effective early warning systems play a crucial role in mitigating their impact
Living in Kelaniya, I faced disruptions in my daily routine because of the sudden flood situation. Traffic jams, road closures, and other challenges led me to conduct a preliminary analysis to grasp the current situation better and assess its impact on the area.
This preliminary analysis was conducted on data from the Kelani River Basin, encompassing four tributaries: Kelani Ganga, Gurugoda Oya, Seethawaka Ganga, and Kehelgamu Oya. The data used for analysis was sourced from Sri Lanka’s Disaster Management Centre (DMC), comprising water level readings from six stations: N’Street, Hanwella, Glencourse, Kitulgala, Holombuwa, Deraniyagala, and Norwood, which monitor the aforementioned tributaries.





Figure 1: Locations of the six selected monitoring stations in the Kelani Ganga basin. The graphical representation was created using the R celyon package developed by Thiyanga S. Talagala, available at https://github.com/thiyangt/ceylon




Upon closer examination of the data for the Kelani River Basin, it was evident that the existing thresholds for early flood warnings are set too high. This caused delays in alerting communities at risk, leading to floods happening “unexpectedly” and making the damage worse. As indicated by the following visual representations covering the seven stations, although the data suggests early warning signs through an increase in water level compared to the historical data, the existing alert thresholds are significantly higher than the observed data. Consequently, this discrepancy has resulted in a failure to issue timely alerts, despite the data clearly indicating an impending disaster.





Figure 2: Water levels at the N’Street Gauging Station and the existing alert levels for minor flood and major flood conditions









Figure 3: Water levels at the Hanwella Gauging Station and the existing alert levels for minor flood and major flood conditions









Figure 4: Water levels at the Glencourse Gauging Station and the existing alert levels for minor flood and major flood conditions









Figure 5: Water levels at the Holombuwa Gauging Station and the existing alert levels for minor flood and major flood conditions









Figure 6: Water levels at the Kitulgala Gauging Station and the existing alert levels for minor flood and major flood conditions









Figure 7: Water levels at the Deraniyagala Gauging Station and the existing alert levels for minor flood and major flood conditions









Figure 8: Water levels at the Norwood Gauging Station and the existing alert levels for minor flood and major flood conditions




To address this issue, it is important to revise these existing thresholds promptly. By lowering them from their current levels, we will be able to establish a more precise and proactive warning system. This will empower authorities to notify vulnerable populations earlier, giving them ample time to prepare and evacuate if necessary.
However, while the need to lower thresholds is evident, it’s vital to strike a balance to prevent the risk of false positives. Overly reducing the thresholds could result in unnecessary warnings, leading people to disregard alerts when genuine danger arises. Therefore, finding the optimal balance is essential to ensuring the effectiveness of the warning system while avoiding unnecessary false alarms.
Comprehensive analyses of historical flood patterns, rainfall data, and the topographical characteristics of the affected regions should be taken into consideration when revising the warning threshold. Collaborative efforts between meteorological agencies, disaster management authorities, data scientists, and relevant stakeholders are essential in establishing revised thresholds that reflect the current realities of climate change and its impact on weather patterns. Further, the existing warning thresholds may no longer be sufficient due to increased construction activities. Empowering local communities with the knowledge and resources to respond effectively to flood warnings can significantly reduce the loss of life and property during disasters. The media has a crucial role to play by making the general public aware of the early flood warning issue by disaster management and other responsible authorities promptly.
With the launch of our latest research initiative focused on broadening our coverage, we are committed to improving our understanding and management of flood risks in Sri Lanka by broadening our analytical scope and putting cutting-edge approaches into practice. Our shared goal is to build a community that is better prepared and resilient.

title: About
text:
I am a senior lecturer in the Department of Computational Mathematics, University of Moratuwa. I earned my PhD in statistics from Monash University, Australia, under the supervision of Professor Rob J. Hyndman and Professor Kate Smith-Miles
I’m a fellow of OWSD, a UNESCO program, from 2021 to 2025. Additionally, I co-founded R-Ladies Colombo a local chapter of the R-Ladies Global Organization which aims to promote gender diversity in the R programming community.
My research revolves around Computational Statistics, Anomaly Detection, Time series analysis and forecasting and Statistical Machine Learning. I’m passionate about developing innovative methods and tools to analyze complex data. I am also strongly committed to developing open-source software tools to facilitate reproducible research. You can check out some of my projects here: Visit me on Twitter I post mostly about R, Python, statistics, data science, and science in nature.
From 2021 to 2024, I served as an associate editor for The R Journal. I’ve also contributed as an Associate Investigator at the Australian Research Council’s (ARC) Centre of Excellence for Mathematical and Statistical Frontiers (ACEMS) from 2019 to 2021.
Thiyanga Talagala,PhD in Statistics, Monash University, Australia is my sister.

title: Creating a Project Page with Blocks in Quarto
text: If you’re building a website with Quarto and want to showcase your projects in a clean, responsive grid layout, you’re in the right place. In this blog post, I’ll show you how to create a project page with blocks, each containing a title, description, image, and link to a detailed project page.

title: Creating a Project Page with Blocks in Quarto
section: 📁 Step 1: Organize Your Project Structure
text:
📁 Step 1: Organize Your Project Structure
Let’s assume the following structure for your Quarto website:
project.qmd
projects/
├── project1.qmd
├── project2.qmd
images/
├── project1.png
├── project2.png

project.qmd is your main project listing page.
projects/ contains detailed .qmd files for each project.
images/ contains thumbnails or preview images for each project.

title: Creating a Project Page with Blocks in Quarto
section: 🧱 Step 2: Add a Grid of Project Blocks
text:
🧱 Step 2: Add a Grid of Project Blocks
Inside project.qmd, we’ll use Bootstrap’s grid system (which Quarto supports) to create a responsive layout.
---
title: "My Projects"
format: html
page-layout: full
toc: false
---

# 🚀 My Projects

::: {.grid}

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-6}
![Anomaly Detection](images/project1.png){width=100px style="float:left; margin-right:1em;"}

### Anomaly Detection in Image Streams  
**Description**: A real-time system for identifying anomalies in high-dimensional image data using explainable AI techniques.  
**Tech Stack**: Python, OpenCV, XAI, TensorFlow  
[View Project](projects/project1.qmd)
:::

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-6}
![Outbreak Detection](images/project2.png){width=100px style="float:left; margin-right:1em;"}

### Outbreak Detection from Surveillance Data  
**Description**: A forecasting tool for detecting early warning signals of disease outbreaks using time series and anomaly detection models.  
**Tech Stack**: R, Prophet, Anomalize  
[View Project](projects/project2.qmd)
:::

:::

🔍 Explanation

.grid starts a responsive row of blocks.
.g-col-md-6 means: take half the width on medium and larger screens.
.g-col-12 ensures blocks stack vertically on small screens (Full-width column (single column)).
If you want three columns, for example, you could use {.g-col-4} (4 + 4 + 4 = 12), and so on.
The number 12 comes from the Bootstrap grid system, which Quarto uses under the hood for layout.
![Project Image](...) adds a project thumbnail with a nice float layout.

title: Creating a Project Page with Blocks in Quarto
section: 📝 Step 3: Create Individual Project Pages
text:
📝 Step 3: Create Individual Project Pages
Each projects/projectX.qmd file is a standard Quarto page:
---
title: "Project One"
format: html
---

# Anomaly Detection in Image Streams

This project presents a real-time anomaly detection system for high-dimensional image streams, designed to identify unexpected or suspicious patterns. We leverage explainable AI (XAI) techniques to interpret model predictions and highlight regions of interest in images.


Include any plots, images, or code relevant to this project.
These pages will render as part of your site, with their own URL.

title: Creating a Project Page with Blocks in Quarto
section: ✅ Result
text:
✅ Result
You now have a responsive, visually clean project gallery page, where each block links to a separate project detail page — perfect for portfolios, research showcases, or teaching materials.
